```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>",
  fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4
)
set.seed(20260529)
source(system.file("knitr/fit-cache.R", package = "tulpa"))
```


A parameter is identifiable when different values of it give different
distributions of the data. Two kinds of failure appear in the models tulpa
fits. In an exact alias, two parameters can move together without changing the
likelihood at all, so no amount of data separates them and the model has to
fix one of them by construction. In a weak identification, the likelihood does
change, but slowly, so a hyperparameter is learned only once the design holds
enough regions, locations or groups. This article derives the four cases the
engine handles (the level of an intrinsic field, the level of a varying
coefficient, the BYM2 variance split together with the range and scale of a
Gaussian process, and a random-effect standard deviation), shows how the
engine resolves the exact aliases, and ends with stress tests and the design
numbers they give. It assumes the model syntax of
[Spatial models](spatial-models.html) and [Temporal models](temporal-models.html).
Installation is covered in [Get started](tulpa.html).

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(tulpa)
```

## The intercept and the level of an intrinsic field

Consider $K$ regions joined by an adjacency matrix $W$, and let $D$ be the
diagonal matrix of neighbour counts. Observation $i$ lies in region $r_i$ and
has the linear predictor

$$
\eta_i = \beta_0 + x_i^\top \beta + \phi_{r_i}.
$$

The ICAR prior on the field $\phi = (\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_K)$ has density
proportional to $\exp\{-\tfrac{\tau}{2}\, \phi^\top (D - W)\, \phi\}$. Every row
of $D - W$ sums to zero, so $(D - W)\mathbf{1} = 0$ for the vector of ones
$\mathbf{1}$. Replacing $\phi$ by $\phi + c\mathbf{1}$ therefore leaves the
prior density unchanged, and replacing $\beta_0$ by $\beta_0 - c$ at the same
time leaves every $\eta_i$ unchanged. The likelihood is constant along the
line $(\beta_0 - c, \phi + c\mathbf{1})$ for every real $c$, and the ICAR
prior puts no density on that direction either.

The engine removes the alias with a sum-to-zero constraint,
$\sum_{r=1}^{K} \phi_r = 0$, which picks one point on each such line. The field
then carries only the contrasts between regions, and the intercept carries the
overall level, including any level the true field had. A graph with several
connected components has one zero eigenvalue of $D - W$ per component, so each
component needs its own constraint, and an RW1 time trend is the same
construction on a chain graph.

The simulation below puts a field with a known level on a ring of 25 regions.
The field is a centred wave plus a shift of 0.3, and the intercept is 0.5, so
the model can identify an intercept of 0.8 and a field equal to the centred
wave.

```{r icar-sim}
ring <- function(K) {
  W <- matrix(0, K, K)
  for (i in 1:K) {
    j <- if (i < K) i + 1 else 1
    W[i, j] <- W[j, i] <- 1
  }
  W
}
K <- 25
W <- ring(K)
wave <- as.numeric(scale(sin(2 * pi * (1:K) / K)))
set.seed(1)
n <- 600
x <- rnorm(n)
region <- sample(1:K, n, replace = TRUE)
y <- rpois(n, exp(0.5 + 0.4 * x + wave[region] + 0.3))
d_icar <- data.frame(y = y, x = x, region = factor(region))
```

Fit the field by nested Laplace and read the intercept and slope.

```{r icar-fit, fit = c("fit_icar")}
fit_icar <- tulpa(y ~ x + spatial(region), data = d_icar,
                  family = "poisson",
                  spatial = list(type = "icar", adjacency = W),
                  mode = "nested_laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
coef(summary(fit_icar))
```

The intercept interval contains 0.8, the intercept plus the shift, and the
slope interval contains 0.4. Each cell of the outer grid holds one inner
Laplace mode, whose columns after the fixed effects are the 25 field values
(`tulpa_outer_grid()`). Their sums show the constraint at every cell.

```{r icar-constraint}
g <- tulpa_outer_grid(fit_icar)
field_cells <- g$modes[, g$n_fixed + seq_len(K)]
range(rowSums(field_cells))
field_hat <- colSums(g$weights * field_cells)
cor(field_hat, wave)
```

The field sums to zero up to rounding error in every cell, and the
grid-averaged field tracks the centred wave. The shift of 0.3 cannot be
recovered as a property of the field: the data contain it only as part of the
intercept.

## The level of a varying coefficient

A varying coefficient lets a slope change over time or space. With a
coefficient $w(t)$ on a covariate $x$, the linear predictor is

$$
\eta_i = \beta_0 + x_i \bigl(\beta_1 + w(t_i)\bigr).
$$

Replacing $w$ by $w + c$ and $\beta_1$ by $\beta_1 - c$ leaves
$x_i(\beta_1 + w(t_i))$, and so $\eta_i$, unchanged for every value of $x_i$.
This is the same alias as in the previous section, moved from the intercept to
a slope. Which instrument removes it depends on the prior on $w$:

- For an intrinsic prior (`rw1`, `rw2`), the constant direction carries no
  prior density, so the engine supplies the missing constraint: it augments
  the precision on the constant direction and pins $\sum_t w(t) = 0$, as for
  the ICAR field.
- For a proper prior (`ar1`, `gp`), the constant direction already carries a
  prior, with precision $\mathbf{1}^\top \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{1}$ for the field
  covariance $\Sigma$. Nothing needs to be added to the prior. The engine
  instead removes the direction from the likelihood by centring the field on
  its way into $\eta$, so the linear predictor uses $w(t) - \bar{w}$, with
  $\bar{w}$ the mean over the time points.

In both cases $\beta_1$ is the average coefficient over the time points and
$w$ is the departure from it. The simulation below uses 30 time points with 20
observations each, a wave of amplitude 0.4 shifted up by 0.25 as the true
$w$, and $\beta_1 = 0.5$. The identifiable slope is therefore $0.5 + 0.25 =
0.75$.

```{r tvc-sim}
set.seed(5)
n_time <- 30
time <- rep(1:n_time, each = 20)
w_true <- 0.4 * sin(2 * pi * (1:n_time) / n_time) + 0.25
x <- rnorm(length(time))
y <- rpois(length(time), exp(0.5 + (0.5 + w_true[time]) * x))
d_tvc <- data.frame(y = y, x = x, time = time)
```

Fit the coefficient once with an intrinsic `rw1` prior and once with a proper
`ar1` prior. Both fits run the NUTS sampler, here with two chains.

```{r tvc-fit, message = FALSE, fit = c("fit_tvc")}
fit_tvc <- lapply(c(rw1 = "rw1", ar1 = "ar1"), function(s) {
  tulpa(y ~ x, data = d_tvc, family = "poisson",
        temporal = temporal_tvc("time", terms = ~ x - 1, structure = s),
        mode = "hmc", control = list(n_chains = 2, seed = 1))
})
t(sapply(fit_tvc, function(f) coef(summary(f))["x", ]))
```

Both slope intervals contain 0.75, the slope plus the mean of $w$. The stored
draws of the field are centred to match, which the sum over time points of
each draw shows.

```{r tvc-centred}
sapply(fit_tvc, function(f) {
  w_draws <- f$draws[, grep("^tvc_w", colnames(f$draws))]
  range(rowSums(w_draws))
})
```

The two priors split the predictor the same way, so the slope means the same
thing under either structure. A reported slope from a varying-coefficient fit
is the average coefficient over the time points, never the coefficient at a
reference time. [Varying coefficients](varying-coefficients.html) covers the
spatial version of this term.

## Weakly identified variance components

The next three cases have no exact alias. The likelihood does depend on each
parameter, but it changes slowly along one direction, so the posterior along
that direction stays wide until the design carries enough information.

### The BYM2 split between structured and unstructured variance

BYM2 writes the field for region $r$ as

$$
\phi_r = \sigma \bigl(\sqrt{\rho}\, u_r^{\star} + \sqrt{1 - \rho}\, v_r\bigr),
$$

where $u^{\star}$ is an ICAR field scaled so that the geometric mean of its
marginal variances is one (Riebler et al. 2016), $v$ is an independent
standard normal effect per region, $\sigma$ is the overall standard deviation
and $\rho \in [0, 1]$ is the share of variance that is spatially structured.
The marginal variance of a region's effect is
$\sigma^2 \bigl(\rho\, s_r + 1 - \rho\bigr)$, where $s_r$ is the scaled ICAR
variance at region $r$. Because the $s_r$ average to one on the log scale,
this variance depends on $\rho$ only weakly, and $\sigma$ is set by the spread
of the effects. The parameter $\rho$ enters mainly through the covariance
between neighbours, $\sigma^2 \rho\, \Sigma^{\star}_{rs}$, so it is learned from
how much more alike neighbouring regions are than distant ones. Each region
contributes one noisy effect to that comparison, and the information on $\rho$
grows with the number of regions.

### Range and marginal standard deviation of a Gaussian process

A continuous field with exponential covariance has

$$
\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(w(s), w(s')\bigr) = \sigma^2 \exp(-d / \phi),
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the locations $s$ and $s'$, $\sigma^2$ the
marginal variance and $\phi$ the range. When the locations stay inside a fixed
region and only become denser, $\sigma^2$ and $\phi$ cannot both be estimated
consistently; only the ratio $\sigma^2 / \phi$ can (Zhang 2004). The reason is
visible at short distances. For small $d$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}\bigl(w(s) - w(s')\bigr) = 2\sigma^2\bigl(1 - e^{-d/\phi}\bigr)
\approx 2 \frac{\sigma^2}{\phi}\, d,
$$

so dense data pin down how rough the field is, which is the ratio. A larger
range with a proportionally larger variance gives almost the same roughness,
and only the behaviour at distances comparable to the size of the region
separates the two. This means that adding locations to the same region should
narrow the posterior of $\log(\sigma^2/\phi)$ much faster than the posteriors
of $\log \sigma^2$ and $\log \phi$. The same holds for a Matern field with
smoothness $\nu$, where the identified quantity is
$\sigma^2 / \phi^{2\nu}$.

### Random-effect standard deviation with few groups

For a random intercept $(1 \mid g)$ the group effects are
$b_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ for groups $j = 1, \ldots, J$. Everything
the data say about $\sigma$ passes through these $J$ effects. Even if the
$b_j$ were observed exactly, the sample variance $s^2$ would satisfy
$(J - 1)\, s^2 / \sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{J-1}$, so the standard deviation of
$\log s$ is close to $1 / \sqrt{2(J - 1)}$: 0.50 at three groups and 0.16 at
twenty. Observations within a group only sharpen each $b_j$; they cannot add
groups. With few groups the interval for $\sigma$ is wide whatever the number
of observations, and the prior on $\sigma$ has a larger share in it.

## Stress tests

Each test below simulates data with known parameters at increasing sizes,
refits, and plots the interval of the hyperparameter against the truth. The
replicate counts are small so the article renders quickly; the numbers in the
design section come from these runs and carry their seeds.

### Random-effect standard deviation against the number of groups

The simulation draws $J$ groups of 10 Poisson observations each, with
intercept 0.3, slope 0.5 and a group standard deviation of 0.7. The fit uses
`mode = "structured"`, which integrates the random-effect scale on an outer
grid. Twenty replicates (seeds 1 to 20) run at each of $J = 3, 5, 10, 20, 40$.

```{r re-one}
re_one <- function(J, seed, m = 10, sigma = 0.7) {
  set.seed(seed)
  grp <- rep(seq_len(J), each = m)
  b <- rnorm(J, 0, sigma)
  x <- rnorm(J * m)
  d <- data.frame(y = rpois(J * m, exp(0.3 + 0.5 * x + b[grp])),
                  x = x, g = factor(grp))
  f <- tulpa(y ~ x + (1 | g), data = d, family = "poisson",
             mode = "structured", control = list(n_threads = 2))
  h <- summary(f)$hyperparameters
  h <- h[h$parameter == "sigma_1", ]
  data.frame(J = J, seed = seed, mean = h$mean, lo = h$ci_lo, hi = h$ci_hi)
}
```

```{r re-run, fit = c("J_set", "re", "re_tab")}
J_set <- c(3, 5, 10, 20, 40)
re <- do.call(rbind, lapply(J_set, function(J) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:20, function(s) re_one(J, s)))
}))
re$covers <- re$lo <= 0.7 & re$hi >= 0.7
re_tab <- aggregate(cbind(covers, width = hi - lo) ~ J, data = re,
                    FUN = function(v) round(median(v), 2))
re_tab$covers <- aggregate(covers ~ J, data = re, FUN = sum)$covers
re_tab
```

`covers` counts the replicates (of 20) whose 95% interval contains 0.7, and
`width` is the median interval width.

```{r re-plot, fig.alt = "95 percent intervals for the random-effect standard deviation in 20 replicates at 3, 5, 10, 20 and 40 groups, with the true value 0.7 as a horizontal line; intervals narrow as the number of groups grows"}
xpos <- match(re$J, J_set) + (re$seed - 10.5) / 30
plot(xpos, re$mean, ylim = range(c(re$lo, re$hi)), pch = 19, cex = 0.5,
     xaxt = "n", xlab = "number of groups J",
     ylab = "random-effect SD")
axis(1, at = seq_along(J_set), labels = J_set)
segments(xpos, re$lo, xpos, re$hi, col = "grey40")
abline(h = 0.7, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
```

At `r J_set[1]` groups the median interval is `r re_tab$width[1]` wide, more than twice the
true value, and the median lower end is `r round(median(re$lo[re$J == 3]), 2)`. At
`r J_set[5]` groups the median width is `r re_tab$width[5]`. Of the `r nrow(re)`
intervals, `r sum(re$covers)` contain 0.7. With few groups the failure is
the width: the intervals still contain the truth but are too wide to say much
about $\sigma$.

### The BYM2 mixing parameter against the number of regions

The regions are square lattices of 4 x 4, 7 x 7, 10 x 10 and 14 x 14 cells,
each joined to its edge neighbours. The true field is a BYM2 draw with
$\sigma = 0.6$ and $\rho = 0.5$, built from the eigen-decomposition of
$D - W$ and the scaling of Riebler et al. (2016). Each region carries 10
Poisson observations with intercept 1 and slope 0.3. Four replicates
(seeds 1 to 4) run at each size.

<details><summary>Simulation code</summary>

```{r bym2-helpers}
lattice <- function(k) {
  W <- matrix(0, k * k, k * k)
  id <- function(i, j) (i - 1) * k + j
  for (i in 1:k) for (j in 1:k) {
    if (i < k) W[id(i, j), id(i + 1, j)] <- W[id(i + 1, j), id(i, j)] <- 1
    if (j < k) W[id(i, j), id(i, j + 1)] <- W[id(i, j + 1), id(i, j)] <- 1
  }
  W
}
draw_bym2 <- function(W, sigma, rho) {
  e <- eigen(diag(rowSums(W)) - W, symmetric = TRUE)
  keep <- e$values > 1e-8
  V <- e$vectors[, keep]
  Qinv <- V %*% (t(V) / e$values[keep])
  scale_u <- exp(mean(log(diag(Qinv))))
  u <- as.numeric(V %*% (rnorm(sum(keep)) / sqrt(e$values[keep])))
  sigma * (sqrt(rho) * u / sqrt(scale_u) + sqrt(1 - rho) * rnorm(nrow(W)))
}
```

</details>

```{r bym2-one}
bym2_one <- function(k, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  W <- lattice(k)
  phi <- draw_bym2(W, sigma = 0.6, rho = 0.5)
  r <- rep(seq_len(k * k), each = 10)
  x <- rnorm(length(r))
  d <- data.frame(y = rpois(length(r), exp(1 + 0.3 * x + phi[r])),
                  x = x, region = factor(r))
  f <- tulpa(y ~ x + spatial(region), data = d, family = "poisson",
             spatial = spatial_bym2(W, group_var = "region"),
             mode = "nested_laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
  h <- summary(f)$hyperparameters
  cbind(K = k * k, seed = seed, h[, c("parameter", "mean", "ci_lo", "ci_hi")])
}
```

```{r bym2-run, fit = c("k_set", "bym")}
k_set <- c(4, 7, 10, 14)
bym <- do.call(rbind, lapply(k_set, function(k) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:4, function(s) bym2_one(k, s)))
}))
bym$width <- bym$ci_hi - bym$ci_lo
aggregate(width ~ parameter + K, data = bym, FUN = function(v) round(median(v), 2))
```

```{r bym2-plot, fig.alt = "95 percent intervals for the BYM2 mixing parameter rho in four replicates at 16, 49, 100 and 196 regions, with the true value 0.5 as a horizontal line; the intervals cover most of the unit interval at 16 regions and narrow with more regions"}
rb <- bym[bym$parameter == "rho", ]
K_set <- k_set^2
xpos <- match(rb$K, K_set) + (rb$seed - 2.5) / 10
plot(xpos, rb$mean, ylim = c(0, 1), pch = 19, xaxt = "n",
     xlab = "number of regions K", ylab = "mixing parameter rho")
axis(1, at = seq_along(K_set), labels = K_set)
segments(xpos, rb$ci_lo, xpos, rb$ci_hi, col = "grey40")
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
```

```{r bym2-numbers, include = FALSE}
rho_w <- aggregate(width ~ K, data = rb, FUN = median)
sig_w <- aggregate(width ~ K, data = bym[bym$parameter == "sigma", ],
                   FUN = median)
rho_cover <- sum(rb$ci_lo <= 0.5 & rb$ci_hi >= 0.5)
```

The median width of the $\rho$ interval is `r round(rho_w$width[1], 2)` at 16
regions, so the data barely move the posterior away from the whole unit
interval, and `r round(rho_w$width[4], 2)` at 196 regions. The interval for
$\sigma$ is much narrower from the start (`r round(sig_w$width[1], 2)` at 16
regions, `r round(sig_w$width[4], 2)` at 196), which matches the derivation:
the overall spread of the effects informs $\sigma$ directly, while $\rho$ needs
many neighbour comparisons. Of the 16 $\rho$ intervals, `r rho_cover`
contain 0.5.

### Range and variance of a Gaussian process against the number of locations

The locations are uniform on the unit square, $n = 100, 200, 400, 800$. The
true field has exponential covariance with $\sigma^2 = 0.64$ and range
$\phi = 0.3$, drawn exactly by a Cholesky factor of its covariance matrix, and
the response is Poisson with intercept 1 and slope 0.3. The fit is the
nearest-neighbour GP of `spatial_gp()` by nested Laplace, with
`scale_coords = FALSE` so that the range is reported in the units of the
square. Three replicates (seeds 1 to 3) run at each size. Each fit integrates
$(\sigma^2, \phi)$ on an outer grid, and `tulpa_outer_grid()` returns its cells
and weights, from which the posterior mean and standard deviation of
$\log\phi$, $\log\sigma^2$ and $\log(\sigma^2/\phi)$ follow as weighted
moments.

```{r gp-one}
gp_one <- function(n, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  co <- data.frame(lon = runif(n), lat = runif(n))
  S <- 0.64 * exp(-as.matrix(dist(co)) / 0.3)
  w <- as.numeric(t(chol(S + diag(1e-8, n))) %*% rnorm(n))
  d <- data.frame(co, x = rnorm(n))
  d$y <- rpois(n, exp(1 + 0.3 * d$x + w))
  f <- tulpa(y ~ x, data = d, family = "poisson",
             spatial = spatial_gp(~ lon + lat, scale_coords = FALSE),
             mode = "nested_laplace", control = list(n_threads = 2))
  g <- tulpa_outer_grid(f)
  L <- cbind(log_phi = log(g$nodes[, "phi_gp"]),
             log_sigma2 = log(g$nodes[, "sigma2"]))
  L <- cbind(L, log_ratio = L[, "log_sigma2"] - L[, "log_phi"])
  m <- colSums(g$weights * L)
  s <- sqrt(colSums(g$weights * sweep(L, 2, m)^2))
  data.frame(n = n, seed = seed, qty = colnames(L), mean = m, sd = s)
}
```

```{r gp-run, fit = c("n_set", "gp", "gp_tab")}
n_set <- c(100, 200, 400, 800)
gp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(n_set, function(n) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(s) gp_one(n, s)))
}))
gp_tab <- aggregate(sd ~ qty + n, data = gp,
                    FUN = function(v) round(median(v), 2))
reshape(gp_tab, idvar = "n", timevar = "qty", direction = "wide")
```

The table gives the median posterior standard deviation on the log scale over
the three replicates. The plot shows each replicate's mean plus and minus two
standard deviations against the truth.

```{r gp-plot, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Three panels for log range, log variance and log of their ratio, each showing posterior mean plus and minus two standard deviations in three replicates at 100, 200, 400 and 800 locations, with the true value as a horizontal line; only the ratio narrows clearly with more locations"}
truth <- c(log_phi = log(0.3), log_sigma2 = log(0.64),
           log_ratio = log(0.64 / 0.3))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (q in names(truth)) {
  gq <- gp[gp$qty == q, ]
  xpos <- match(gq$n, n_set) + (gq$seed - 2) / 8
  ylim <- range(gp$mean - 2 * gp$sd, gp$mean + 2 * gp$sd)
  plot(xpos, gq$mean, ylim = ylim, pch = 19, xaxt = "n",
       xlab = "locations n", ylab = q, main = q)
  axis(1, at = seq_along(n_set), labels = n_set)
  segments(xpos, gq$mean - 2 * gq$sd, xpos, gq$mean + 2 * gq$sd,
           col = "grey40")
  abline(h = truth[q], lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
}
par(op)
```

```{r gp-numbers, include = FALSE}
sd_at <- function(q, n) gp_tab$sd[gp_tab$qty == q & gp_tab$n == n]
```

From 100 to 800 locations the median posterior standard deviation of
$\log(\sigma^2/\phi)$ falls from `r sd_at("log_ratio", 100)` to
`r sd_at("log_ratio", 800)`, while that of $\log\phi$ stays between
`r min(gp_tab$sd[gp_tab$qty == "log_phi"])` and
`r max(gp_tab$sd[gp_tab$qty == "log_phi"])` and that of $\log\sigma^2$
between `r min(gp_tab$sd[gp_tab$qty == "log_sigma2"])` and
`r max(gp_tab$sd[gp_tab$qty == "log_sigma2"])`.

## Design recommendations

The numbers below come from the stress tests above, with their seeds and
replicate counts; they describe these simulations and are a starting point for
a design check on your own model, which repeats a test like these at your
own sample sizes and effect sizes.

- **Random-effect SD.** With 10 Poisson observations per group and a true SD
  of 0.7 (20 replicates per size), the median 95% interval for the SD was
  `r re_tab$width[re_tab$J == 3]` wide at 3 groups,
  `r re_tab$width[re_tab$J == 5]` at 5, `r re_tab$width[re_tab$J == 10]` at 10
  and `r re_tab$width[re_tab$J == 20]` at 20. The derivation gives the floor:
  even with the effects known, the standard deviation of the log SD is about
  $1/\sqrt{2(J-1)}$, so more observations per group cannot replace groups.
  With a handful of groups, report the interval, read its upper end as prior
  information, or treat the groups as fixed effects.
- **BYM2 mixing parameter.** At 16 regions the median $\rho$ interval was
  `r round(rho_w$width[1], 2)` wide on a unit interval, and at 196 regions
  `r round(rho_w$width[4], 2)` (4 replicates per size, 10 observations per
  region). On maps of a few dozen regions, read $\rho$ as weakly informed and
  base conclusions on $\sigma$ and the fitted field; an ICAR field
  ([Spatial models](spatial-models.html)) drops the parameter.
- **Gaussian-process range and variance.** Inside a fixed unit square, going
  from 100 to 800 locations reduced the posterior SD of
  $\log(\sigma^2/\phi)$ from `r sd_at("log_ratio", 100)` to
  `r sd_at("log_ratio", 800)` and left those of $\log\phi$ and $\log\sigma^2$
  at `r sd_at("log_phi", 800)` and `r sd_at("log_sigma2", 800)` (3 replicates
  per size). Denser sampling in the same region identifies the ratio. By the
  derivation, the range is informed separately by distances comparable to
  the size of the region, which this test did not vary; the prior on it
  ([Priors](priors.html)) carries the rest. Report the range with its interval and avoid
  conclusions that depend on the range alone.
- **Intercept and field level.** Under an ICAR, RW1 or varying-coefficient
  term the intercept or slope carries the level of the field, so it is the
  quantity to report and compare. A shift of the true field shows up in the
  fixed effect, as the 0.3 shift did in the intercept above.
